extracted.intended_audience: historians of mathematics, philologists, textual critics, and scholars preparing or using critical editions of classical mathematical texts (Archimedes)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating the provenance, relationships, and reliability of manuscripts, translations, and editions of Archimedes’ works, using paleography, concordances, lacunae, external documentary evidence, and collation. Focused on establishing stemma, dating, and editorial quality for classical mathematical texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provenance from ownership-notes and dating
rubrics_metrics.description: Use notes of former ownership to date and relate manuscripts (e.g., 'archetype formerly belonged to George Valla and afterwards to Albertus Pius' → infer B was written before Albertus' death in 1531).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: External ownership annotations and the sequence of named owners provide terminus ante quem/terminus post quem for copying. Example: if a manuscript's note omits a later owner's name who should have been mentioned, infer an earlier copy-date. Be alert to copyists' omissions or later additions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviations as comparative evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Lists of 'peculiar abbreviations used in the archetype' are important 'for the purpose of comparison with F and other MSS.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare distinctive abbreviation systems across MSS to establish common ancestry or direct copying. Unique or rare abbreviation forms are strong stemmatic markers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scribe-colophon details (scribe, date, patron)
rubrics_metrics.description: Notes stating who wrote a manuscript, where and when, and for whom (e.g., 'that MS. was written by one Christophorus Auverus at Rome in 1544, at the expense of Georgius Armagniacus').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat explicit colophon-like notes as primary evidence of origin; cross-check with external documentary sources about named patrons or commissions to corroborate.

rubrics_metrics.name: External documentary references linking MS to historical events/libraries
rubrics_metrics.description: Use letters and published accounts (e.g., Philander's letter mentioning a volume 'destined to adorn the library founded by Francis at Fontainebleau' and 'had been the property of George Valla') to identify or confirm a manuscript's identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correlate descriptions in contemporaneous letters or printed works with physical features and contents of MSS to link a manuscript to a historical repository or presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shared contents and ordering among MSS
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence of 'the same works of Archimedes and Eutocius, and in the same order' in several MSS (F, B, C) is evidence of relationship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concordant contents and book-order across witnesses support common descent or shared exemplar; differences in order may indicate different transmission lines or editorial rearrangement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common lacunae as sign of common archetype
rubrics_metrics.description: When 'all three MSS. have the same lacuna' (and the copyist notes missing pages), this indicates the defect was in the archetype.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shared gaps (lacunae) are strong evidence of a common defective source; check whether some witnesses fill the lacuna (possible independent recovery) or all repeat the same omission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence/absence of textual completion marks
rubrics_metrics.description: The archetype's legibility at the end may be inferred from the absence of completion marks (e.g., 'there is no word τέλος at the end of F, nor any other of the signs by which copyists usually marked the completion of their task').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for conventional paratextual marks (τέλος, explicit, subscription) — their absence, especially when other witnesses contain them, can indicate a mutilated or illegible exemplar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paleographic dating from letter-forms and abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: The form of letters and abbreviations ('the form of most of the letters in it is older than the 15th century, and the abbreviations etc., ... agree marvellously with the description') are used to date a manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use letter-shapes, abbreviations, and script style to estimate copying date; concordance with described abbreviation-lists strengthens dating and relationship claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreement with early translations as evidence of source
rubrics_metrics.description: Concordance between a manuscript and an early translator's readings (e.g., 'Valla’s translations ... agree completely with the text of F') indicates that the manuscript (or its exemplar) was the translator's source or closely related.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare early Latin (or vernacular) translations and their characteristic readings/errors with MSS to infer which Greek MS the translator used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyist alterations and editorial authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the extent of a copyist's emendations ('the writer of B was somewhat of an expert and made many alterations on his own authority, not always with success').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge a witness's trustworthiness by detecting deliberate corrections, harmonizations, or conjectural emendations by the scribe; such interventions can reduce a witness's value as a faithful witness to the archetype.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shared mistakes as stemmatic markers
rubrics_metrics.description: Mistakes common to particular manuscripts ('Some mistakes common to it and F alone show that its source was F') indicate direct descent or a close relationship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shared unique errors (not mere common sense corrections) are strong evidence for common ancestry; use them to build a stemma codicum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lacuna correspondence between translations and MSS
rubrics_metrics.description: When a translation 'has the same lacuna as that in F, B and C' it suggests the translator used that MS or its exemplar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concordance of lacunae between translations and MSS links the translator's source to those MSS; absence of hints in the translation of an independent reading further supports dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marginal notes, corrections, and printer's directions as evidence of editorial use
rubrics_metrics.description: Notes and erasures by later hands (e.g., Venatorius 'corrected many mistakes ... made many alterations ... and sometimes wrote on it directions to the printer') show active editorial intervention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record and assess later annotations and physical alterations: they reveal how MSS were used in editions and whether the MS served as a compositor's copy, which affects textual history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detection of interpolations and composite sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpolations and inserted material from other MSS (e.g., 'this interpolated copy of F was apparently also the source of the Nurnberg MS.') identify composite witnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spot paraphrases, abridgements, or passages matching other sources to detect composite witnesses; such mixed texts complicate stemma but reveal editorial practice and the circulation of corrected/collated copies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fidelity (or slavish copying) of translations
rubrics_metrics.description: A translator's close copying is evidenced when he reproduces 'most obvious errors and perverse punctuation' of an earlier translation (Tartaglia copying Gauricus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High fidelity to a prior translation, including its errors, indicates direct dependence; use characteristic reproduced errors to link translated editions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of fresh collation for editions
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish editions 'based upon any fresh collation of the MSS.' from those that are not; editions lacking fresh collation are less reliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer editions produced from fresh, careful collation of primary witnesses; note when editors rely on earlier printed texts without collating MSS, as this propagates earlier errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialectal and linguistic features to detect later alteration
rubrics_metrics.description: Loss or preservation of Archimedes' Doric dialect and later interpolations ('Archimedes wrote in the Doric dialect ... traces disappear ... alterations and additions were first of all made by an interpolator') are diagnostic of later editorial activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze dialectal forms and their retention/loss across witnesses to detect interpolations, later recasting, or stages of transmission. Preservation of archaic forms may indicate an earlier stage of the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal cross-references and prefaces to establish chronology
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'prefatory letters' and 'the use in later works of properties proved in earlier treatises' to approximate chronological sequence of works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internal references (citations, reliance on prior propositions) and authorial prefaces provide relative dating of treatises; use these to build an internal chronology when external dating is lacking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content-coherence and presence of expected features for authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge authenticity of fragments by internal criteria (e.g., the Greek fragment 'seems to be of doubtful authenticity. Except for the first proposition, it contains enunciations only and no proofs').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authentic Archimedean material is expected to include demonstrated proofs where appropriate; fragments lacking characteristic methodological features may be later re-translations or non-authentic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stemma reconstruction via comprehensive collation and schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: Reconstruct relations among MSS and editions by compiling a scheme (Heiberg's scheme showing relationships among Codex Vallae, V, B, C, N*, editions etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine paleography, shared errors, lacunae, external documentary evidence, and collation results into an explicit stemma to visualize descent and editorial dependencies; make the stemma explicit in editions.
